extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, educators, and students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying communication theories to design, research, write, and evaluate public relations campaigns and materials; includes theory explanations, audience analysis, media-selection criteria, and case-study examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of theory in public relations campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory provides an important foundation for any type of public relations writing; it provides a framework for turning ideas into plans and plans into campaigns and encourages strategic and critical thinking within well-defined parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theory to identify and narrow the problem, structure research, guide message design, and evaluate outcomes. Without theory there is no coherent map for planning or evaluating PR efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research and problem definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and narrow the problem so that only one specific problem is addressed at any given time; conduct internal and external analysis of organizational elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research must determine root causes (e.g., absenteeism due to environment, morale, management, information flows). If the problem is not clearly defined, solutions may be ineffective; analyze departments, employees, managers, their relationships and communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholeness (General Systems Theory characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A system constitutes a whole; all parts are interrelated and any change in one part affects the whole system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning campaigns, consider organizational parts together rather than in isolation; interventions in one area will ripple through the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence (General Systems Theory characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: All parts of a system are intertwined and affect one another; mutual interaction among parts produces results different from each part individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Campaigns should account for interactions among units (e.g., management, staff, departments) and foster information exchange and joint problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy (General Systems Theory characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems create levels of increasing complexity (e.g., administrators, managers, subordinates); the system operates on levels forming organizational structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize decision-making levels and tailor messages and interventions to appropriate hierarchical audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-regulation and control (General Systems Theory characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of the system behave according to rules and goals and adapt based on feedback; systems maintain themselves through regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design communication processes (feedback loops, reporting) that allow the organization to sense and correct deviations from norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchange with the environment (General Systems Theory characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: The system exchanges information and resources with its environment; this interchange affects organizational success or failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public relations must manage external interactions (community, media, stakeholders) to maintain favorable relations and organizational survival.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance (General Systems Theory characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining equilibrium is a primary task of interacting subsystems; systems must sense and adjust to deviations from the assigned norm or standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use communication strategies to detect imbalances (e.g., power struggles) and restore stability through negotiated adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change and adaptability (General Systems Theory characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations undergo change due to internal or external conditions and must adapt (e.g., reallocate work, reorganize).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan messages and programs that facilitate adaptation, communicate changes clearly, and provide transitional supports (e.g., temporary hires, training).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equifinality (General Systems Theory characteristic)
rubrics_metrics.description: A particular final state can be accomplished in many ways and from many starting points; the system can produce the same output via different processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to multiple strategies to achieve campaign goals (e.g., produce a newsletter via in-house writing, distributed reporters, or outsourcing); select approaches based on context and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information processing as predictor of audience attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: How publics perceive, conceptualize, and integrate new information into their cognitive systems predicts attitude and behavior change; belief changes lead to attitude and behavior changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand audiences' existing belief structures and how new information will complement, contradict, or create beliefs; design messages to facilitate cognitive accommodation and persuasion when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yale attitude approach: Source, Message, Channel, Receiver variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuasive messages are stimuli mediated by cognition; message variables related to the Source, Message, Channel, and Receiver affect persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider source credibility and attractiveness, message content and clarity, choice of channel (including multimodal benefits), and receiver characteristics when designing persuasive communications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiver characteristics affecting persuadability
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuadability is influenced by personality and demographic factors (e.g., age tends to be negatively correlated with persuasion), gender findings vary, and degree of involvement or interest strongly affects susceptibility to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess audience involvement: highly involved individuals are harder to persuade and may require more central-route arguments; novice or less-involved audiences may respond to different tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Channel effects and resource constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Channel choice affects comprehension and persuasion (visual+auditory combos like television often more effective than print/radio alone); distractions and noise interact with persuasion; available resources and local access dictate feasible channels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select channels based on audience media access, distraction level, cost, and message complexity; account for rural/urban differences in media availability and budget limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Learning Theory as a persuasive strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning is social—people observe, admire, emulate, and integrate behaviors; if rewarded for adopted behaviors, attitudes and behaviors consolidate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design campaigns that model desired behaviors (e.g., leaders exemplify sacrifices), create observable rewards or reinforcement, and use modeling to encourage adoption (case study: Potek salary-cut/reward example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Exchange Theory as a persuasive strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Relationships seek equitable exchange; perceived inequity creates tension until corrected—communication programs are needed to address imbalances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure PR programs to create mutually beneficial exchanges (e.g., WHJ bank's school program: teachers received training, bank received customers/publicity); identify and correct perceived resource imbalances via communication and incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-way symmetrical communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Symmetrical interactions occur when communicators share control and exchange information and feedback; such two-way strategies maintain organizational balance and positive relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor two-way communication (surveys, follow-ups, dialogue) over unilateral messaging; use feedback channels and act on input to build trust (case study: Vivian's country club membership growth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coorientation model for defining publics
rubrics_metrics.description: A public is a group aware of shared interests; key elements are degree of self-awareness and orientation toward shared interests—higher perceived agreement eases communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitate communication to increase mutual awareness between organization and publics (e.g., suggestion boxes, staff meetings). Use coorientation to map where publics are informed/aware and tailor outreach accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elaboration-Likelihood Model implications
rubrics_metrics.description: People are persuaded by thinking about and elaborating on messages; individuals differ in prior knowledge and involvement which determines elaboration routes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor messages to audience involvement: central-route messages for high-involvement audiences, peripheral cues for low-involvement groups; consider delivering multiple messages for different segments (case study: Clorise's Respiratory Association used separate messages for adults and children).

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience analysis and profiling (demographic vs psychographic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use research to sketch audience profiles (values, attitudes, lifestyles = psychographics) rather than relying only on demographics (age, sex, religion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey and profile current and prospective publics to determine tailored messaging (example: Vivian's survey produced psychographic traits used to segment and target recruitment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations for choosing media (Newsom, Scott, VanSlyke Turk list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key questions for medium selection: audience media usage and credibility; timing needs; budget/cost constraints; which medium reaches the broadest target segment at lowest cost; medium credibility vs cost; which medium delivers the message within required time; whether to use a single medium or a media mix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answer each question with research-driven evidence (media-use patterns, deadlines, costs, credibility perceptions). Prefer combinations when audiences are heterogeneous; balance cost, credibility, reach, and timeliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of PR writing: inform vs persuade
rubrics_metrics.description: Public relations writing serves to persuade or inform—to create favorable public opinion, educate audiences, or change perceptions and behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about the primary objective (informational vs persuasive) because it affects message structure, evidence levels, and ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Message content, organization, and presentation quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate message content and organization, audience analysis, and quality of message presentation (style, format, mechanics, presentation) are essential for effective PR writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor content and organization to audience needs and chosen medium; attend to clarity, style, tightness for electronic media, and journalistic conventions for print; ensure mechanical correctness and professional format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of case studies and applied examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative case studies (e.g., Potek, WHJ Bank, Vivian's, Clorise's Respiratory Association) demonstrate application of theories to real campaign steps and outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ case-study analysis in planning and teaching to show how theory-guided steps (research, profiling, message design, implementation, feedback) produce measurable results; replicate relevant tactics where contextually appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory characteristics/functions (systematic view and relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory should present a systematic view of observed phenomena and specify relations among variables and how they are related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting or applying a theory, ensure it articulates variables and relationships to structure research and message design; use the theory to link constructs to campaign activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory function: explanation of past/present behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful theory explains past and/or present behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply theory to interpret historical or current audience behaviors as a basis for intervention design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory function: prediction of future behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: A reliable theory predicts, with high probability, future behavior; prediction is the culmination of other theory functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theoretical predictions to set measurable objectives and to design evaluation criteria; confirm theory through successful prediction or revise accordingly.
